check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self to the mother and confirms the child's name and age.
Uses plain language, acknowledges the mother's fear and explains what they are doing.
History
Characterises the illness:

kids.x: Coryza for 2 days, then a barking cough and noisy breathing from about 8 pm, getting worse
Noisy breathing at rest, not only when upset
Fever and how unwell the child seems

check.x: Screens for red flags of other causes:

kids.x: A sudden choking episode or something put in the mouth (inhaled foreign body)
Rash, facial or lip swelling, new food or medicine (anaphylaxis)

check.x: Asks about intake and output: drinking, eating and wet nappies.
Past history: previous croup or stridor, prematurity or airway problems, and immunisation status including Hib.
Medicines, allergies, sick contacts and who is at home.
Explores the mother's ideas, concerns and expectations.
Examination
Keeps the child upright on the mother's lap and observes from a distance first:

kids.x: Inspiratory stridor at rest and barking cough
No drooling, tripod posture or cyanosis

check.x: Assesses work of breathing: respiratory rate, suprasternal and subcostal recession, tracheal tug.
Asks for SpO2, heart rate, capillary refill and temperature.
Does not look in the throat or lie the child flat, and says why: upsetting the child worsens the obstruction, and a tongue depressor can cause complete obstruction if this is epiglottitis.
Listens to the chest and checks hydration.
Interpretation
Classifies the croup on arrival as moderate: stridor at rest with mild to moderate recession in a quiet, consolable child (yellow zone on the chart: clinical review).

Recognises severe croup on reassessment, in the red zone of the chart: agitation, loud stridor at rest, marked recession with tracheal tug, RR 52 and HR 168, and SpO2 91%, a late sign that the airway is close to failing.

Considers epiglottitis, bacterial tracheitis, inhaled foreign body and anaphylaxis, and states what argues against each here (a coryzal start, immunised against Hib, no drooling or toxic look, no choking episode, no allergic features).
States that croup is a clinical diagnosis and that bloods and X-rays are not needed and would distress the child.
Management
Gives nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 (1 mg/mL) now: 5 mL undiluted for 12 kg (5 mL is the maximum; 0.5 mL/kg would be 6 mL), repeated if needed with senior involvement.
Gives oxygen for SpO2 below 92%, aiming for 92% or above, without upsetting the child (through the nebuliser or a mask held near the face on the mother's lap).
Gives a steroid, with the dose for 12 kg:

kids.x: Now (severe croup, no steroid given yet): dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg = 7.2 mg (maximum 12 mg), orally if the child will take it, otherwise IM or IV
Had the croup stayed moderate: oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg = 1.8 mg, or oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg = 12 mg, as a single dose

check.x: Acts on the red zone now: calls a rapid response (in the ED, the senior doctor to the bedside) and moves the child to the resuscitation area; involves ICU and anaesthetics early, given the low SpO2, and for any repeat adrenaline dose or a tiring child.
Reassesses after adrenaline and observes with continuous SpO2 for at least 3 hours after the last dose, because its effect wears off within about 2 hours and the stridor can return.
Explains to the mother that croup is a viral swelling of the upper airway, not asthma, why the adrenaline and the steroid are given, and that the child will stay in hospital tonight.
Safety netting
States discharge criteria: at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline, no stridor at rest and no recession, drinking well, and the mother confident.

Tells the mother to call 000 if the child is struggling to breathe, has blue lips, is pale or drowsy, or is drooling or cannot swallow, and to come straight back to the ED for noisy breathing at rest or the chest sucking in.

Explains that croup usually settles over 3 to 4 days and is often worse at night, arranges GP review if it is not settling by then or keeps coming back, and gives the RCH Kids Health Info croup fact sheet.

desc: This station involves a focused history from the mother and a gentle examination of a 2-year-old with a barking cough and stridor, then interpreting the observations on arrival and on reassessment, classifying the croup, outlining management with weight-based doses, and safety-netting the mother.
explain:
Severity

The RCH CPG grades croup by behaviour, stridor and work of breathing. Mild croup is a barking cough with stridor only when upset, little or no increase in work of breathing and normal behaviour. Moderate croup has stridor at rest, with tracheal tug or chest wall recession and some irritability. Severe croup has stridor at rest with a marked increase in work of breathing and increasing agitation or lethargy. SpO2 often stays normal until late, so hypoxaemia, drowsiness, exhaustion or cyanosis mean the airway is close to failing. Stridor can quieten as a child tires, so a quieter child is not always a better one. This child had moderate croup on arrival and severe croup with hypoxaemia 20 minutes later. On the Standard Paediatric Observation Chart (1 to 4 years) that is the yellow zone on arrival (moderate respiratory distress and the mother's concern: clinical review) and the red zone 20 minutes later (severe respiratory distress, with RR, HR and SpO2 all yellow: rapid response).

Steroids

Give a steroid early to every child with stridor at rest. For moderate croup the RCH dose is a single oral dose of dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg (1.8 mg for 12 kg) or prednisolone 1 mg/kg (12 mg). Mild croup may not need one; consider the same dose if there has been stridor or the family cannot easily get back. Severe croup takes dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, maximum 12 mg (7.2 mg for 12 kg), orally, IM or IV. Steroids take time to work, so a child can still worsen in the first hours.

Severe croup

Nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 (1 mg/mL), 5 mL undiluted, works within minutes; for 12 kg, 0.5 mL/kg capped at 5 mL gives the same 5 mL. Its effect wears off within about 2 hours, so repeat it if needed with senior involvement, and observe for at least 3 hours after the last dose. Give oxygen for SpO2 below 92% without upsetting the child. Severe croup needs senior review in a high-acuity area, with ICU and anaesthetics involved early for hypoxaemia, repeated adrenaline or a tiring child. Life-threatening obstruction needs the resuscitation area, high-flow oxygen and an experienced clinician to secure the airway.

History, examination and investigations

Croup is a clinical diagnosis: a coryzal illness, then a barking cough, hoarse voice and inspiratory stridor, worse at night, usually between 6 months and 6 years of age. The history screens for its dangerous mimics: drooling, difficulty swallowing and a toxic child (epiglottitis, now rare after Hib immunisation; bacterial tracheitis, with high fever and a poor response to adrenaline), a sudden choking episode (inhaled foreign body) and allergic features (anaphylaxis). Examine from a distance with the child upright on the parent's lap and do not look in the throat: distress worsens the obstruction, and a tongue depressor can cause complete obstruction in epiglottitis. Bloods and X-rays are not needed and upset the child.

Disposition and safety netting

A child who needed adrenaline is observed for at least 3 hours after the last dose and can go home only when there is no stridor at rest, they are drinking well and the parent is confident. This child, with severe croup and a low SpO2 at night, stays in hospital tonight. The RCH Kids Health Info croup fact sheet gives the advice: call 000 for a child who is struggling to breathe, pale or drowsy, has blue lips, or is drooling or cannot swallow; see a doctor urgently for stridor at rest or the chest sucking in. Croup usually settles over 3 to 4 days and is often worse at night; see the GP if it is not settling or keeps coming back.
focus: Croup in a toddler with stridor
guide:
In Part 1, the mother answers the history and the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they would examine. In Part 2, hand over the results and ask the questions in order. No medicines have been given before the reassessment.

A high-performing candidate screens for the dangerous mimics in the history, examines from a distance with the child on the mother's lap and leaves the throat alone, classifies moderate croup on arrival and severe croup on reassessment, and gives nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL, oxygen for SpO2 below 92%, dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (7.2 mg) and an early senior and ICU call. They give specific discharge criteria (at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline, no stridor at rest) and red flags.

For the moderate-croup steroid, the RCH dose is dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg (1.8 mg) or prednisolone 1 mg/kg (12 mg); accept up to 0.3 mg/kg (3.6 mg) if the arithmetic is right. For adrenaline, 5 mL reached as 0.5 mL/kg capped at 5 mL is also correct.

A borderline candidate identifies croup but miscalculates a dose, delays adrenaline or escalation, upsets the child, or gives vague safety netting such as "come back if worse".
patient:
Role: You are the mother of a 2-year-old (12 kg). You are worried and tired. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they would examine. If the candidate tries to look in the throat or lie the child down, say the child is screaming and the noisy breathing is much worse.

Opening line: "Their breathing sounds terrible, like a seal barking, and it is getting worse."

History (give only when asked):

  • Runny nose and mild fever for 2 days. The barking cough and noisy breathing started at about 8 pm and are worse when the child cries or is upset.
  • The noisy breathing is there even when the child is sitting quietly on your lap now.
  • Highest temperature at home 38 °C. Not floppy, still interacting with you.
  • Drinking smaller amounts than usual, about half; 2 wet nappies today. Has eaten a little.
  • No drooling, swallowing normally. No choking episode, no small toys or food missing, nothing put in the mouth before it started.
  • Hoarse cry. No rash, no swelling of lips or face, no new foods or medicines.
  • No previous episodes like this. Born at term, no breathing problems as a baby, no hospital admissions.
  • Fully immunised, including the 18-month vaccines. No regular medicines. No allergies.
  • Older sibling at childcare had a cold last week. Lives with both parents, no smokers at home.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you think it might be asthma, like your nephew. You are scared the child will stop breathing tonight. You hope for medicine and to go home.

Questions to ask if there is time: "Is this serious?" "Why can't you look in the throat?" "Can we go home tonight?"
points: Moderate croup: a single oral dose of dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg (1.8 mg for 12 kg) or prednisolone 1 mg/kg (12 mg); severe croup: dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg, maximum 12 mg (7.2 mg for 12 kg).
Severe croup: nebulised adrenaline 1:1000, 5 mL undiluted, with senior help in a high-acuity area and ICU and anaesthetics early for hypoxaemia or repeated doses.
Hypoxaemia is a late sign in croup; give oxygen for SpO2 below 92% without upsetting the child.
Observe for at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline dose; discharge needs no stridor at rest.
Keep the child calm and upright on the parent's lap; no tongue depressor, bloods or X-rays in typical croup.
refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Croup (fact sheet)
stem: You are the junior doctor in a metropolitan Emergency Department at night. A 2-year-old child weighing 12 kg has been brought in by their mother with a barking cough and noisy breathing. The child is sitting on the mother's lap. A nurse is with you.
tasks: Take a focused history from the mother and perform a focused examination of the child, telling the examiner what you are examining and why. Keep the child calm (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you the child's observations on arrival and on reassessment. Interpret them, then outline your management approach, with doses for this child, and your safety netting (5 minutes).
title: Toddler with stridor: croup

part2.lead: Here are the observations on arrival. No medicines have been given yet. While you were finishing your assessment, the nurse reassessed the child 20 minutes later.

handover.label: Observations on arrival and 20 minutes later

rows.note: Inspiratory stridor at rest, mild to moderate suprasternal and subcostal recession; quiet and consolable on mother's lap.
Agitated, hard to settle; loud stridor at rest, marked recession with tracheal tug; no drooling. Doctor asked to review now.

handover.model:
22:40, arrival (SPOC 1 to 4 years): RR 36, SpO2 96% in room air, HR 138, BP 95/60, temperature 37.8 °C, CRT 2 s and alert are all in the white zone. Moderate respiratory distress (stridor at rest with recession) and the mother's concern are yellow: yellow zone, clinical review. Clinically this is moderate croup: stridor at rest in a quiet, consolable child.

23:00, no medicines yet: severe respiratory distress (agitated, loud stridor at rest, marked recession, tracheal tug) is red, and RR 52, HR 168, SpO2 91% and the mother's concern are each yellow (3 or more yellows is a red criterion on its own): red zone, rapid response now. This is severe croup, and the falling SpO2 is a late sign that the airway is close to failing.

It changes the plan at once: nebulised adrenaline 1:1000 5 mL, oxygen without upsetting the child, dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (7.2 mg), and senior, ICU and anaesthetic help with the child moved to the resuscitation area.

handover.label: Investigations
handover.result: No blood tests, swabs or imaging have been done.
handover.model: None are needed. Croup is a clinical diagnosis (coryza, then a barking cough, hoarse cry and inspiratory stridor in a 2-year-old), and bloods, a swab or a neck or chest X-ray would not change management, while upsetting the child worsens the obstruction. Think again only if the course is atypical, such as a toxic child or a poor response to adrenaline (bacterial tracheitis), and then only once the airway is safe. If the candidate asks for a test, the examiner says it is not indicated and would distress the child.

ask: You are now calling the paediatric registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of this child, including your interpretation of these observations.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of this child now, here in the emergency department, with doses for this child.
Before this child goes home, what would you tell the mother and what follow-up would you arrange?
expect:
• Identify: ED junior doctor; 2-year-old, 12 kg, here with mother.
  • Situation: severe croup, now in the red zone with SpO2 91%. I need you to review now.
  • Background: 2 days of coryza and fever to 38 °C, then barking cough and stridor from 8 pm; fully immunised including Hib; no drooling, choking or allergic features; no medicines given yet.
  • Assessment: 22:40 moderate croup (stridor at rest, mild to moderate recession, consolable, SpO2 96%): yellow zone. 23:00 severe croup (agitated, loud stridor, marked recession, tracheal tug, RR 52, HR 168, SpO2 91%): red zone; hypoxaemia is a late sign that the airway is close to failing. No tests needed.
  • Recommendation: giving nebulised adrenaline 5 mL, oxygen and dexamethasone 7.2 mg; moving to resus; please come now; involve ICU and anaesthetics early.

Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), severe on reassessment: age 2, coryzal start, barking cough, hoarse cry, inspiratory stridor worse at night, low-grade fever. It is a clinical diagnosis, so no bloods or X-rays.

  • Epiglottitis: against: immunised against Hib, no drooling, swallowing normally, not toxic, began with coryza.
  • Bacterial tracheitis: against: only low-grade fever, not toxic. Consider it if the child responds poorly to adrenaline.
  • Inhaled foreign body: against: no choking episode, nothing put in the mouth, gradual onset after coryza.
  • Anaphylaxis: against: no rash, no lip or facial swelling, no new food or medicine.

1. Keep the child calm and upright on the mother's lap; do not examine the throat or lie the child flat.
  2. Red zone: call a rapid response (senior doctor to the bedside) and move to resus.
  3. Nebulised adrenaline 1:1000, 5 mL undiluted (0.5 mL/kg capped at 5 mL); repeat if needed with senior involvement.
  4. Oxygen for SpO2 below 92%, aiming for 92% or above, through the nebuliser or a mask held near the face.
  5. Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg = 7.2 mg (maximum 12 mg), orally, otherwise IM or IV. Had it stayed moderate: oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg = 1.8 mg, or prednisolone 1 mg/kg = 12 mg.
  6. Involve ICU and anaesthetics early because of the low SpO2, any repeat adrenaline or a tiring child.
  7. Reassess, use continuous SpO2 and observe for at least 3 hours after the last adrenaline; admit tonight.
  8. Explain to the mother: viral airway swelling, not asthma.

• Discharge only when: it is at least 3 hours since the last adrenaline, there is no stridor at rest and no recession, the child is drinking well and the mother feels confident. Tonight the child stays in hospital.
  • Call 000 if: your child is struggling to breathe, has blue lips, is pale or drowsy, or is drooling or cannot swallow.
  • Come straight back to ED for: noisy breathing at rest, or the chest sucking in.
  • Course: it usually settles over 3 to 4 days and is often worse at night.
  • Follow-up: see the GP if it is not settling by then or keeps coming back. Give the RCH Kids Health Info croup fact sheet.
